etymology: Hebrew Pishon, from a root meaning to leap forth or spread abroad; the overflowing river, the first of the four heads into which the river of Eden parted.
biblical_def: Pison is the first of the four rivers that watered the garden of Eden, “that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold” (Gen 2:11), and the gold of that land is good, with bdellium and the onyx stone (Gen 2:12). Here is paradise as it came from the hand of God, unfallen and undefiled, a garden made glad by a river that parted into four heads and enriched the earth with gold and precious stone. Yet the Pison flows now only in the record of what was lost. When Adam sinned, the way to the tree of life was barred, the cherubim and the flaming sword set at the east of the garden, and the rivers of Eden passed out of the reach of fallen men. We cannot find the Pison; we cannot walk down to Havilah; the gold of innocence is spent. But what the first Adam forfeited, the last Adam restores. For the Spirit sheweth at the last a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev 22:1), and by it the tree of life bearing her fruit. The Pison teaches us to mourn the paradise lost in our father, and to thirst for the better Eden secured in Christ, where the river never fails and the curse is no more.
webster_summary: The first river of Eden, compassing Havilah, the land of good gold, bdellium, and onyx (Gen 2:11); a witness to paradise lost in Adam and the river of life restored in Christ.
webster_full: PISON, the first of the four rivers of Eden.

The rivers of Eden were lost to men when the way to the tree of life was barred.
A figure of the pure river of water of life restored in the last Eden.

corruption_paragraphs: A lost river of Eden raises no partisan quarrel, and none is manufactured here. The Pison is named that we may remember what was, and what shall be again in Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that paradise was real and is truly lost in Adam — not a myth of the childhood of the race, but a garden watered by four rivers, forfeited by one man’s transgression. Let the soul mourn the loss and thirst for the pure river of water of life that proceeds out of the throne of God and of the Lamb, secured for His people by the last Adam.

etymology: Hebrew Chiddeqel, the swift or rapid river; the third river of Eden, known to later ages as the Tigris.
biblical_def: Hiddekel is the third of Eden’s four rivers, “that is it which goeth toward the east of Assyria” (Gen 2:14), the great stream that later ages called the Tigris. It rose in paradise, where every river ran pure; but the same channel that watered the garden of God flowed on into the land of Asshur, into the country of Babel and Nineveh, into the very heart of the world’s captivity. And there, by the bank of that far river, the LORD did not fall silent. “In the four and twentieth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which is Hiddekel” (Dan 10:4), Daniel lifted up his eyes and beheld a Man clothed in linen, His body like the beryl, His face as the appearance of lightning — a vision of the glorious Christ granted to an exile in a strange land. Here is the comfort of the Hiddekel: the word of the LORD is not bound. It runs from Eden to Babylon; it finds His servant beside a heathen river; it visits the captive with revelations of glory. Though His people be carried far from the place of worship, God is not carried away from them. He who walked in the garden in the cool of the day speaks yet by the great river, and gives to those who mourn in exile the vision of His Son.
webster_summary: The third river of Eden, the Tigris (Gen 2:14); by its far bank Daniel the exile beheld the vision of the glorious Man (Dan 10:4).
webster_full: HIDDEKEL, the third river of Eden, going toward the east of Assyria.

A witness that the word of the LORD runs even to Babylon.

corruption_paragraphs: The Hiddekel raises no modern grievance; it is named to comfort the captive. From Eden it flowed to Babylon, and there the LORD met His prophet.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the word of the LORD is not bound by distance or exile. He who set the rivers of Eden speaks yet by the great river Hiddekel, granting to Daniel the vision of the glorious Christ. Let the pilgrim far from the sanctuary know that God is not carried away from His people, but visits them with His Son wherever they are scattered.

etymology: Hebrew Shichor, from a root meaning black or dusky; the dark, turbid water before Egypt, reckoned the south-west border of the land of promise.
biblical_def: Shihor, the dark and turbid water before Egypt, marked the south-west border of the land of promise: “From Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward” (Jos 13:3). It was the frontier stream toward the house of bondage, and Jeremiah takes it up as a rebuke: “what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor?” (Jer 2:18). Judah, forsaking her God, ran down to Egypt for help, stooping to sip the muddy Nile as though its dark waters could quench the thirst of the soul. This is the two-fold evil the LORD laid to His people’s charge: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13). Shihor preaches the folly of every heart that turns from the clear and living Spring to the turbid streams of the world. The Nile runs thick with mud and rises only to fall; the broken cistern leaks out what little it holds; but the fountain of living waters never fails. Christ cries, “If any man thirst, let him come unto me and drink.” To leave that fountain for the Shihor is to exchange the river of God for the ditch of Egypt, and to die athirst beside the very water that cannot save.
webster_summary: The dark water before Egypt, the south-west border of the land (Jos 13:3); Jeremiah rebukes Judah for going to drink its waters instead of the fountain of living waters (Jer 2:18).
webster_full: SHIHOR, the dark water before Egypt, on the south-west border of the land.

A figure of the broken cisterns men hew out in the room of God.

corruption_summary: The muddy water of Egypt that Judah preferred to her God; it exposes the perennial sin of forsaking the fountain of living waters for the broken cisterns of the world.
corruption_paragraphs: Here a genuine corruption of the heart is laid bare, older than any modern error and never out of season. The LORD is the fountain of living waters, clear, near, and unfailing; yet His people turned their backs upon Him and went the way of Egypt to drink the dark waters of Sihor. The idols of the age are not always graven; often they are the muddy streams men trust in the room of God — the arm of the strong, the wisdom of the world, the pleasures that promise and cannot pay. Every such choice is Judah’s two-fold evil: forsaking the Spring, and hewing out cisterns that hold no water.

The principle to recover is that God alone is the fountain of living waters, and every substitute is a broken cistern. Let the soul not go down to Egypt, nor stoop to the turbid Nile, but come to Christ, who cries, “If any man thirst, let him come unto me and drink.” The waters of Sihor cannot save; the water that He gives springs up into everlasting life. Turn from the ditch of the world to the river of God, and thirst no more.

etymology: Hebrew Chabor, from a root meaning to join or bind together; the river of Gozan in Assyria, a place of Israel’s captivity.
biblical_def: Habor was the river of Gozan in the land of Assyria whither the ten tribes were carried when Samaria fell: the king of Assyria “carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan” (2Ki 17:6). By this far stream the covenant curse came to its bitter fulfilment. Long before, in the law, the LORD had warned that if His people would not hearken He would scatter them among the heathen and draw out a sword after them; and now, by Habor’s waters, the sentence fell. The God of Israel Himself “stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria…and he carried them away” (1Ch 5:26) — not the arm of the heathen only, but the hand of a holy God chastening a people that forsook Him. Yet even in the place of exile the mercy of the covenant is not spent. He who passes His people through the waters is with them: “when thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee” (Isa 43:2). Habor teaches the dread seriousness of forsaking the LORD, for He will surely visit transgression with the rod; yet it teaches also that He preserves a remnant, and that no river of exile runs beyond the reach of His faithfulness.
webster_summary: The river of Gozan in Assyria to which the ten tribes were carried captive (2Ki 17:6); a witness to the covenant curse of exile and to the LORD who yet preserves a remnant.

corruption_paragraphs: A river of the ancient captivity raises no fashionable dispute, and none is invented. Habor is named that we may feel both the terror and the mercy of the covenant.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD chastens the sin of His people in earnest — He carried the ten tribes to Habor by His own hand, that His threatenings are no idle words. Yet the same God is with His own even in the waters, and no river of exile overflows those He has chosen. Fear His rod, and rest in His faithfulness to preserve a remnant according to the election of grace.

etymology: Hebrew Gozan, from a root meaning to cut off or shear; the Mesopotamian region and river to which the northern tribes were deported.
biblical_def: Gozan was the Mesopotamian region, watered by the river of the same name, into which the northern tribes were deported: they were placed “in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes” (2Ki 17:6). It became a byword in the mouth of the proud Assyrian. When the Rabshakeh stood before Jerusalem and blasphemed, he numbered Gozan among the lands whose gods had not delivered them: “Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad?…have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand?” (2Ki 18:34). The taunt was true against the idols and a lie against the living God. The gods of the nations are vanity; they are the work of men’s hands, and they save none. Gozan’s idols could not keep Gozan, and Samaria’s calves could not keep Samaria. But Assyria reasoned as the heathen ever do, that the LORD of hosts was but one more helpless god among the wooden many. That blasphemy the Lord answered in a night. Gozan stands therefore as a double witness: the scattering was foretold in the law and came to pass, so that the vanity of Israel’s idolatry was laid bare; and the vanity of the nations’ idols was laid bare also, that men might know there is no God beside the LORD, who alone delivers and alone destroys.
webster_summary: The Mesopotamian region of Israel’s deportation (2Ki 17:6); the Rabshakeh taunted that its gods could not deliver, a lie against the living God.

corruption_summary: The region of Israel’s scattering; it recovers the vanity of idols and the sole godhead of the LORD who delivers and destroys.
corruption_paragraphs: A region of the old deportations stirs no current controversy, and none is contrived. Gozan is named that we may weigh both the fulfilment of the law and the emptiness of every idol.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gods of the nations are vanity and the LORD alone is God. The scattering to Gozan came to pass just as the law foretold, exposing the folly of Israel’s calves; and the Rabshakeh’s taunt, true of idols, was blasphemy against the living God, and was answered in a night. Fear no idol of the age, and trust the God who alone delivers His people and destroys their enemies.

etymology: Hebrew Qishon, from a root meaning to bend or wind; the winding river of the plain of Esdraelon, called that ancient river.
biblical_def: The river Kishon runs through the plain of Esdraelon, and across its bed was fought one of the great deliverances of the Judges. The LORD said to Barak, “I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army, with his chariots and his multitude; and I will deliver him into thine hand” (Jdg 4:7). The nine hundred chariots of iron came down to the water, and there the God of heaven fought for Israel. The rains fell, the river rose, and the boasted chariots were mired and swept to ruin: “The river of Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. O my soul, thou hast trodden down strength” (Jdg 5:21). Here is a lesson writ in water: the whole creation is armed for the battles of the LORD. He needs no legions; a swollen brook is enough to undo an army. The stars in their courses fought against Sisera, and the ancient river carried off his host. Let the mighty of the earth trust in their chariots; the people of God sing of Him who overthrows them with a flood. As Deborah’s song ascends, so should ours, for the same LORD subdues the enemies of His church and treads down their strength, and the day comes when every proud confederacy against His Anointed shall be swept away as by the river Kishon.
webster_summary: The winding river of Esdraelon that swept away Sisera’s host at Deborah’s battle (Jdg 5:21); a witness that creation itself is armed for the battles of the LORD.

corruption_paragraphs: A river of triumph in the days of the Judges raises no modern quarrel, and none is fabricated. Kishon is named that we may sing with Deborah of the LORD who fights for His people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the whole creation is armed for the battles of the LORD. He needed no host at Kishon; a swollen brook undid nine hundred chariots of iron. Let the mighty trust in their engines; the church trusts in the God who treads down strength, and will yet sweep away every confederacy against His Anointed as the ancient river swept away Sisera.

etymology: Hebrew Arnon, from a root meaning to roar or rush; the deep gorge-river that formed the border of Moab.
biblical_def: Arnon is the deep gorge-river that formed the border of Moab, and Israel came to it in the last stage of the wilderness march: they “pitched on the other side of Arnon…for Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites” (Num 21:13). What the LORD wrought there was thought worthy of a sacred chronicle now lost to us, “the book of the wars of the LORD”: “Wherefore it is said in the book of the wars of the LORD, What he did in the Red sea, and in the brooks of Arnon” (Num 21:14). The Red sea and the brooks of Arnon are set side by side, the opening and the closing victories of the pilgrimage, both the doing of the same mighty hand. For the LORD is a man of war. He sets the bounds of the nations and appoints their habitations; He gives Moab its border and Israel its inheritance; He fights the battles of His people and writes their triumphs in His book. Arnon teaches the pilgrim that the God who divided the sea will divide every last river, and that the wars of the way are the wars of the LORD. Those whom He redeems out of Egypt He also brings in over Arnon, and not one of His promised borders shall fail, for He is faithful that hath said it, and He will surely do it.
webster_summary: The gorge-river border of Moab, named in the book of the wars of the LORD (Num 21:14); a witness that the LORD sets the bounds of nations and wins His people’s battles.

corruption_paragraphs: A border-river of the wilderness march raises no partisan dispute, and none is manufactured. Arnon is named that we may see the LORD as the man of war who brings His people in.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD sets the bounds of the nations and fights the battles of His people. The Red sea and the brooks of Arnon stand together in His book, the first and last victories of the pilgrimage by the same almighty hand. He who redeems His people out of Egypt will surely bring them in over every river, for not one of His promised borders shall fail.

etymology: Hebrew Meribah, from a root meaning to strive or contend; the waters of strife, where Israel chided with the LORD.
biblical_def: At Meribah, the waters of strife, Israel came again to the old sin of murmuring, and there the meekest of men was overtaken. “This is the water of Meribah; because the children of Israel strove with the LORD, and he was sanctified in them” (Num 20:13). The congregation chode with Moses for want of water, and God commanded him to speak to the rock; but Moses, provoked, smote it twice and took to himself and Aaron the glory: “must we fetch you water out of this rock?” For this the LORD barred him from Canaan: “ye rebelled against my word at the water of Meribah” (Num 20:24). Yet mark the mercy in the midst of the chiding: the rock gave forth its water still. Provocation was answered with grace, and the smitten rock poured out a river in the desert. For “that Rock was Christ” (1Co 10:4). The Rock smitten in the wilderness is our Lord, stricken for our transgressions, out of whose riven side flow living waters to a rebellious and thirsty people. Meribah preaches two solemn things at once: the seriousness of dishonouring God before the people, so that even Moses felt the rod; and the wonder of a grace that gives drink to the very murmurers who deserve to die of thirst. The Rock was smitten once; now His people have but to ask, and the water flows.
webster_summary: The waters of strife where Israel chided and Moses smote the rock and was barred from Canaan (Num 20:13); the Rock was Christ (1Co 10:4), smitten to pour forth living water.
webster_full: MERIBAH, the waters of strife in the wilderness.

Yet the smitten rock poured forth water to the thirsty congregation.
That Rock was Christ, stricken to give living water to His people.
scriptures: This is the water of Meribah; because the children of Israel strove with the LORD, and he was sanctified in them.
Aaron shall be gathered unto his people: for he shall not enter into the land which I have given unto the children of Israel, because ye rebelled against my word at the water of Meribah.
And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.
Psa 81:7
Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee; I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah.
corruption_summary: The waters of strife where the smitten rock gave drink to murmurers; it recovers the seriousness of dishonouring God and the grace of the Rock that is Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The waters of strife raise no fashionable dispute, and none is contrived. Meribah is named that we may fear to dishonour God and marvel at the Rock that was smitten for us.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: the LORD is jealous for His glory, so that even Moses, for smiting the rock and robbing God of praise, was shut out of Canaan; and yet the smitten Rock gave water to the very murmurers, for that Rock was Christ. Fear to dishonour Him before His people; and drink freely of the living water that flows from His riven side.
roots_summary: Hebrew Meribah, from the root riyb, to strive or contend; strife, chiding, contention.
roots_lines: Meribah — Hebrew Meribah, that is, Strife (Num 20:13).
From the root riyb, to strive, chide, or contend.
Paired with Massah, temptation, at the rock in Horeb.
Named again at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.
Recalled in the Psalms as the place where God proved His people.
usage: This is the water of Meribah, where Israel strove with the LORD.
Moses was barred from Canaan for his sin at the water of Meribah.
The Rock smitten at Meribah was Christ, who gives living water.

etymology: The spring of the city of Jericho (Hebrew Yeriycho), whose naught and barren waters Elisha healed with salt in a new cruse.
biblical_def: When Elisha came to Jericho the men of the city told him of a grief that lay upon the place: “the situation of this city is pleasant…but the water is naught, and the ground barren” (2Ki 2:19). The spring itself was corrupt, and a poisoned spring poisons every field it feeds; the fair city sat by deadly water. The prophet did not treat the fields but went to the fountain-head. He cast salt from a new cruse into the spring and spake the word of the LORD: “I have healed these waters; there shall not be from thence any more death or barren land” (2Ki 2:21). And so it was: “the waters were healed unto this day” (2Ki 2:22). Here is a bright figure of regenerating grace. The trouble of a man is not in the branches but at the spring; out of the heart are the issues of life, and the heart by nature is naught, sending forth death and barrenness through the whole of the life. Salvation goes to the source. The word of the LORD, applied by His Spirit, heals the fountain of the heart, so that the streams run sweet and the barren ground bears fruit unto God. What the salt in the new cruse did for Jericho’s spring, the grace of the new covenant does for the sinner: it makes the bitter well whole, and there is no more death.
webster_summary: The naught and barren spring of Jericho that Elisha healed with salt in a new cruse (2Ki 2:21); a figure of regenerating grace at the spring of the heart.
webster_full: WATERS OF JERICHO, the spring of the city of Jericho.
The water was naught and the ground barren, though the city was pleasant.
Elisha cast salt from a new cruse into the spring.
By the word of the LORD the waters were healed, and death and barrenness ceased.
A figure of grace that heals the fountain of the heart.
scriptures: And the men of the city said unto Elisha, Behold, I pray thee, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord seeth: but the water is naught, and the ground barren.
And he went forth unto the spring of the waters, and cast the salt in there, and said, Thus saith the LORD, I have healed these waters; there shall not be from thence any more death or barren land.
So the waters were healed unto this day, according to the saying of Elisha which he spake.
Eze 47:9

And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh.
corruption_summary: The healed spring of Jericho; it recovers the truth that grace heals the fountain of the heart, not merely the outward life.
corruption_paragraphs: A healed spring in the days of Elisha raises no current dispute, and none is invented. The waters of Jericho are named that we may see how grace works at the source.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that man’s malady lies at the spring and not in the branches, for out of the heart are the issues of life. No mending of outward conduct can heal a poisoned fountain; the word of the LORD, applied by His Spirit, must make the spring itself whole. As the salt in the new cruse healed Jericho’s water, so regenerating grace heals the heart, and the streams thereof run sweet unto God.
roots_summary: The waters (Hebrew mayim) of Jericho; the spring whose bitterness Elisha healed by the word of the LORD.
roots_lines: Waters of Jericho — the spring of the city of Jericho (2Ki 2:19).
Hebrew mayim, waters, joined to the name Jericho.
The water was “naught,” and the ground “causing to miscarry.”
Healed by salt cast from a new cruse with the word of the LORD.
Distinct from the city of Jericho itself; here the spring is in view.
usage: The waters of Jericho were naught, and the ground barren.
Elisha healed the waters of Jericho with salt in a new cruse.
The healed waters of Jericho figure grace at the spring of the heart.

etymology: Hebrew Bor Sirah, the well or cistern of Sirah, from a root meaning to turn aside; the well whence Joab recalled Abner to slay him.
biblical_def: The well of Sirah is remembered for a deed of blood. Abner, captain of Israel’s host, had come in peace to David and gone away under safe conduct; but Joab, hearing of it, “sent messengers after Abner, which brought him again from the well of Sirah: but David knew it not” (2Sa 3:26). At the gate Joab took him aside as if to speak quietly, and smote him under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother. It was murder cloaked as justice, private vengeance masquerading as the avenging of blood. The well of Sirah stands therefore as a warning against the vengeful heart. Joab would not wait upon the LORD nor upon the appointed way; he took the sword into his own hand and stained himself with blood-guilt that clung to him to his dying day. But vengeance is not ours to take: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” God had set cities of refuge in Israel, that the manslayer might flee and the avenger be restrained, and that innocent blood and guilty might be sifted by lawful judgment, not by the passion of a wronged man. David, who was our Refuge’s figure, mourned Abner and left the recompence to God. Let no man carry Joab’s quarrel; let him flee rather to the true City of Refuge, and leave the reckoning to the righteous Judge.
webster_summary: The well from which Joab treacherously recalled Abner and slew him for his brother’s blood (2Sa 3:26); a warning against private vengeance and blood-guilt.
webster_full: WELL OF SIRAH, the well whence Joab recalled Abner.
Abner had departed from David in peace, under safe conduct.
Joab sent messengers and brought him again, David not knowing it.
At the gate Joab smote him for the blood of Asahel his brother.
A warning against the vengeful heart and the guilt of shed blood.
scriptures: And when Joab was come out from David, he sent messengers after Abner, which brought him again from the well of Sirah: but David knew it not.
Joab also and Abishai pursued after Abner: and the sun went down when they were come to the hill of Ammah, that lieth before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon.
And the children of Benjamin gathered themselves together after Abner, and became one troop, and stood on the top of an hill.
Psa 46:1
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
corruption_summary: The well where Abner was murdered for private revenge; it recovers the peril of blood-guilt and the LORD’s claim, Vengeance is mine.
corruption_paragraphs: A deed of blood at an ancient well raises no fashionable dispute, and none is manufactured. The well of Sirah is named that we may abhor private vengeance and honour the God who judges righteously.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that vengeance belongs to God alone. Joab, refusing the appointed way, made himself a murderer under colour of avenging his brother, and the blood-guilt followed him to the grave. The LORD had set cities of refuge that judgment might be lawful and the avenger restrained. Let no man take the sword into his own hand, but flee to the true City of Refuge, and leave the recompence to the righteous Judge who has said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.”
roots_summary: Hebrew Bor Sirah, the well or cistern of Sirah, from a root meaning to turn aside; a place near Hebron.

Remembered solely for the treacherous slaying of Abner.
usage: Joab brought Abner again from the well of Sirah, but David knew it not.

The well of Sirah warns against the vengeful heart and its blood-guilt.
